  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.

  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }

    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.

    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");

  }

  initializeReadingPreferences();

<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">ReHear: Iterative Pseudo-Label Refinement for Semi-Supervised
<br class="ltx_break">Speech Recognition via Audio Large Language Models</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Zefang
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Chenyang
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Sangwoo
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Shi-Xiong
</span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Semi-supervised learning in automatic speech recognition (ASR) typically relies on pseudo-labeling, which often suffers from confirmation bias and error accumulation due to noisy supervision. To address this limitation, we propose ReHear, a framework for iterative pseudo-label refinement that integrates an instruction-tuned, audio-aware large language model (LLM) into the self-training loop. Unlike conventional text-based correctors, our approach conditions the LLM on both the ASR hypothesis and the source audio, allowing it to recover phonetically accurate transcripts even from severe recognition errors. These refined pseudo-labels serve as high-fidelity targets for fine-tuning the ASR model in an iterative cycle. Experimental results across diverse benchmarks demonstrate that ReHear effectively mitigates error propagation, consistently outperforming both supervised and pseudo-labeling baselines.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_classification"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_classification">keywords</h6>automatic speech recognition, large language models, semi-supervised learning, pseudo-labeling
</div><span id="id1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_address"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">address: </span><sup id="id1.1" class="ltx_sup">1</sup> Capital One, USA</span></span></span><span id="id2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_email"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">email: </span>zefang.liu@capitalone.com</span></span></span>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">End-to-end (E2E) automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>, exemplified by models like Conformer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite>, Whisper <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>, and OLMoASR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite>, have achieved state-of-the-art performance across a wide range of benchmarks. Although the utilization of massive, often weakly supervised web-scale datasets has endowed these models with impressive general capabilities, adapting them to the distinct acoustic and linguistic nuances of specific downstream tasks remains a significant challenge. Achieving high precision in specialized domains, distinct accents, or low-resource languages typically demands high-quality, human-annotated data. Consequently, the prohibitive cost and scarcity of such ground-truth labels create a significant bottleneck, severely limiting the effective deployment of these powerful models in scenarios where labeled data is sparse but unlabeled audio is abundant.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To mitigate the reliance on labeled data, semi-supervised learning (SSL), particularly through pseudo-labeling (PL), has emerged as a prevalent strategy. In this framework, a “teacher” ASR model generates transcriptions for a large corpus of unlabeled audio, which subsequently serve as targets to fine-tune a “student” model. However, the efficacy of this approach is fundamentally limited by error propagation. As the teacher model is prone to misrecognitions, training the student on these noisy pseudo-labels can reinforce errors and destabilize the optimization process. Although various filtering strategies based on confidence scores or uncertainty estimation have been proposed to curate the training data, they are often suboptimal; by discarding samples with low-confidence labels, these methods forfeit potentially valuable acoustic information contained in the discarded audio.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18721v1/rehear.svg" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/245;" width="476" height="245"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>Overview of the proposed ReHear framework. The pipeline employs an audio-aware LLM to refine hypotheses via multimodal context, subsequently using these refined pseudo-labels to iteratively fine-tune the ASR model on data.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we diverge from the traditional filtering paradigm and instead propose to actively refine noisy pseudo-labels. We introduce <span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ReHear</span>, a novel semi-supervised ASR framework that leverages the emergent capabilities of multimodal audio large language models (Audio LLMs) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>, <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>. As illustrated in Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ ReHear: Iterative Pseudo-Label Refinement for Semi-SupervisedSpeech Recognition via Audio Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, our approach employs a multimodal corrector that conditions on both the initial ASR hypothesis and the raw source audio. By grounding corrections directly in the acoustic signal, the model can disambiguate phonetic uncertainties and rectify errors that are intractable for text-only correctors. Specifically, we establish a collaborative loop between a base ASR model and an Audio LLM, where the latter refines the ASR’s initial predictions to generate high-fidelity targets for subsequent fine-tuning. This cycle fosters a self-improving dynamic, enabling the ASR system to effectively exploit large-scale unlabeled data while progressively mitigating error propagation. Ultimately, ReHear offers a robust and data-efficient pathway to adapt ASR systems to new domains without the need for extensive human annotation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Pseudo-labeling (PL) has become a dominant paradigm for semi-supervised ASR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>, significantly advanced by iterative pseudo-labeling (IPL) strategies where targets are continuously re-generated during training <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite>. This process has been further refined through teacher-student frameworks utilizing exponential moving average (EMA) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite> or momentum-based updates <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite>, alongside techniques for improved stability such as dynamic caching <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite> and convergent teacher initialization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite>. To mitigate error propagation from noisy labels, standard approaches typically filter unlabeled data based on uncertainty metrics <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>, <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite>, confidence scores <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite>, or multi-model consensus <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite>. Diverging from simple filtering, recent research attempts to actively correct noisy labels, utilizing methods ranging from modified CTC objectives <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite>, hybrid decoding strategies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>, and parameter-space bias correction <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite> to LLMs serving as post-processors <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite>. These include text-only denoising LMs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite> and multimodal speech LLMs that leverage source audio for correction <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite>. Building on this, we propose an alternating iterative loop where an audio-aware LLM acts as a corrector to refine pseudo-labels for ASR fine-tuning. Unlike prior works that rely on complex ensembles or require computationally expensive Audio LLMs for run-time inference, our approach distills the corrector’s knowledge directly into the ASR model, ensuring the final deployed system remains lightweight and efficient.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Methodology</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our proposed <span id="S3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ReHear</span> framework orchestrates a self-improving training loop between a primary ASR model, denoted as <math id="S3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{A}</annotation></semantics></math>, and an audio-aware LLM functioning as a corrector, denoted as <math id="S3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{L}</annotation></semantics></math>. As outlined in Algorithm <a href="#alg1" title="Algorithm 1 ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ ReHear: Iterative Pseudo-Label Refinement for Semi-SupervisedSpeech Recognition via Audio Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, the protocol iterates through four sequential stages: ASR inference, LLM training, LLM inference, and ASR training. This cyclic design fosters a symbiotic relationship where the two models mutually reinforce one another: an improved ASR model supplies more accurate initial hypotheses, which enables the corrector to generate higher-fidelity pseudo-labels for subsequent ASR optimization.</p>
</div>
<figure id="alg1" class="ltx_float ltx_float_algorithm ltx_framed ltx_framed_top">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_float"><span id="alg1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Algorithm 1</span> </span> ReHear: Iterative Pseudo-Label Refinement</figcaption>

</figure>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In the initial <span id="S3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ASR inference</span> stage, the current ASR model <math id="S3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{A}</annotation></semantics></math> generates hypotheses for both the labeled dataset <math id="S3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{L}=\{(x_{l},y_{l})\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{L}=\{(x_{l},y_{l})\}</annotation></semantics></math> and the unlabeled dataset <math id="S3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{U}=\{x_{u}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>U</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{U}=\{x_{u}\}</annotation></semantics></math>. For the labeled data, this yields triplets <math id="S3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(x_{l},y_{l},y^{\prime}_{l})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>y</mi><mi>l</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x_{l},y_{l},y^{\prime}_{l})</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y^{\prime}_{l}=M_{A}(x_{l})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>y</mi><mi>l</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y^{\prime}_{l}=M_{A}(x_{l})</annotation></semantics></math>, which serve as training examples for the corrector. Simultaneously, initial noisy pseudo-labels <math id="S3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y^{\prime}_{u}=M_{A}(x_{u})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>y</mi><mi>u</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y^{\prime}_{u}=M_{A}(x_{u})</annotation></semantics></math> are generated for the unlabeled data to act as input for correction. Subsequently, in the <span id="S3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LLM training</span> stage, the Audio LLM <math id="S3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{L}</annotation></semantics></math> is fine-tuned to perform ASR error correction. Specifically, it learns to map the multimodal inputs, comprising the audio <math id="S3.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> and the hypothesis <math id="S3.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y^{\prime}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>y</mi><mi>l</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y^{\prime}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math>, to the ground truth <math id="S3.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> by minimizing the causal language modeling loss <math id="S3.p2.m11" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{LLM}=-\sum\log P(y_{l}\mid x_{l},\mathcal{T}(y^{\prime}_{l});\theta_{L})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></msub><mo rspace="0em">=</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.055em">−</mo><mo>∑</mo><mi>log</mi><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>y</mi><mi>l</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>;</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{LLM}=-\sum\log P(y_{l}\mid x_{l},\mathcal{T}(y^{\prime}_{l});\theta_{L})</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{T}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{T}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> represents a prompt template wrapping the hypothesis. This step effectively conditions the LLM to identify and repair specific error patterns produced by the ASR model, leveraging both acoustic evidence and linguistic priors. The process then advances to the <span id="S3.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LLM inference</span> stage, where the fine-tuned <math id="S3.p2.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{L}</annotation></semantics></math> rectifies the noisy pseudo-labels <math id="S3.p2.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y^{\prime}_{u}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>y</mi><mi>u</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y^{\prime}_{u}</annotation></semantics></math> from the unlabeled set, producing refined transcriptions <math id="S3.p2.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y^{\prime\prime}_{u}=M_{L}(x_{u},\mathcal{T}(y^{\prime}_{u}))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>y</mi><mi>u</mi><mo>′′</mo></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>y</mi><mi>u</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y^{\prime\prime}_{u}=M_{L}(x_{u},\mathcal{T}(y^{\prime}_{u}))</annotation></semantics></math>. To safeguard quality, an optional filtering mechanism removes corrections exhibiting signs of hallucination or excessive deviation, resulting in a high-fidelity subset <math id="S3.p2.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D^{f}_{U}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>D</mi><mi>U</mi><mi>f</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D^{f}_{U}</annotation></semantics></math>. Finally, in the <span id="S3.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ASR training</span> stage, <math id="S3.p2.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{A}</annotation></semantics></math> is fine-tuned on a combined corpus of the original labeled data and the filtered, corrected pseudo-labels. The objective minimizes <math id="S3.p2.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{ASR}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>S</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{ASR}</annotation></semantics></math>, defined as a sum of the supervised loss on <math id="S3.p2.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{L}</annotation></semantics></math> and the semi-supervised loss on <math id="S3.p2.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D^{f}_{U}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>D</mi><mi>U</mi><mi>f</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D^{f}_{U}</annotation></semantics></math>. This updated <math id="S3.p2.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{A}</annotation></semantics></math> is then carried over to the next cycle, closing the loop. The iterative process terminates when a predefined maximum iteration count is reached or when validation performance saturates.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To further safeguard the training process against occasional hallucinations generated by the LLM, we explore two filtering strategies. The first is a heuristic rule-based mechanism that imposes constraints on character deviation and length consistency relative to the original ASR hypothesis, rejecting samples that exhibit significant divergence or repetition loops. The second is a model-based approach where a pre-trained text encoder is fine-tuned as a binary classifier to predict whether a given correction yields a lower word error rate (WER) than the initial hypothesis. In summary, by integrating this audio-aware correction, which can be optionally augmented by robust filtering, ReHear mitigates the noise accumulation typical of standard pseudo-labeling. This enables the ASR model to progressively leverage unlabeled data for sustained performance gains.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experiments</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we outline the experimental setup, including dataset and implementation specifics, followed by a comprehensive analysis of the main results and ablation studies.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Datasets</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To evaluate the efficacy of our proposed method in challenging real-world contexts, we utilize four specialized corpora: Earnings-21 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite>, Earnings-22 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite>, SPGISpeech <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>]</cite>, and the AMI Meeting Corpus <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>, <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite>. Earnings-21 provides approximately <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="39" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>39</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">39</annotation></semantics></math> hours of earnings calls across nine financial sectors, serving as a benchmark for entity-dense speech and named entity recognition. Building on this, Earnings-22 introduces <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="119" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>119</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">119</annotation></semantics></math> hours of recordings from global companies, specifically designed to test system robustness against diverse international accents. We also incorporate SPGISpeech, a large-scale corpus originally containing <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5,000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>5,000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5,000</annotation></semantics></math> hours of formatted earnings calls; to facilitate efficient experimental iteration, we employ a representative sampled subset. Finally, to assess generalization to spontaneous conversational speech, we include the AMI corpus, which comprises <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>100</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">100</annotation></semantics></math> hours of multi-party meeting recordings characterized by unscripted dynamics and frequent disfluencies. All corpora consist of English speech, encompassing diverse domains and accents. Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4.1 Datasets ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ReHear: Iterative Pseudo-Label Refinement for Semi-SupervisedSpeech Recognition via Audio Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> summarizes the detailed statistics and partition splits for the datasets used in our experiments.</p>
</div>

</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Data Preparation</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We tailor our preprocessing pipeline to handle the distinct formats of the corpora. For the long-form Earnings-21 and Earnings-22 datasets, we standardize raw recordings to <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>16</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">16</annotation></semantics></math>kHz and normalize transcripts by mapping non-speech annotations (e.g., laughter) to unified special tags. To generate training-ready samples, we employ a segmentation pipeline using a pre-trained Wav2Vec 2.0 model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>]</cite> coupled with CTC segmentation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>, <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>]</cite>. We utilize sliding window inference for acoustic probabilities and align them with text using a backtracking window of <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8,000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>8,000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8,000</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="100,000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>100,000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">100,000</annotation></semantics></math> frames. Adjacent segments with silence gaps under <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math>s are merged, targeting a maximum chunk duration of <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="30" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>30</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">30</annotation></semantics></math>s after adding <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.1</annotation></semantics></math>s boundary padding. Conversely, for the pre-segmented SPGISpeech and AMI corpora, we bypass alignment and focus on consistency. The SPGISpeech dataset (small version) is downsampled to create a representative subset: we sample <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10\%</annotation></semantics></math> of the training set for labeled data and <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="30\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>30</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">30\%</annotation></semantics></math> for unlabeled, while retaining <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10\%</annotation></semantics></math> of both validation and test splits. For AMI independent headset microphones (IHM), we perform session-level partitioning by selecting <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="20\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>20</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">20\%</annotation></semantics></math> of the original training sessions as the labeled set and assigning the remainder to the unlabeled set. To maintain data quality, we apply rigorous filtering to discard segments shorter than <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.05" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.05</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.05</annotation></semantics></math>s, longer than <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="30" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>30</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">30</annotation></semantics></math>s, or containing empty transcripts. Across all datasets, partitioning is strictly managed at the source file or meeting level to ensure no speaker or context leakage occurs between splits.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Prompt Templates</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To adapt the LLM for the ASR correction task and ensure the output meets pseudo-labeling requirements (i.e., transcription only), we design specific instruction templates. For the primary audio-aware correction, we instruct the model to ground its output in acoustic features using the following template: <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">“Correct the ASR hypothesis based on the provided audio. Transcribe the speech exactly as spoken. Output strictly the corrected text without any explanations or fillers. Hypothesis: <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&lt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>&lt;</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&lt;</annotation></semantics></math>hypothesis<math id="S4.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&gt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>&gt;</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&gt;</annotation></semantics></math>”</span>, where <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&lt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>&lt;</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&lt;</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">hypothesis<math id="S4.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&gt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>&gt;</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&gt;</annotation></semantics></math></span> is a placeholder for the ASR hypothesis. For the text-only variant where audio is unavailable, we modify this template by replacing the first two sentences with linguistic constraints: <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">“Correct the ASR hypothesis by fixing typos and misspellings. Preserve the original style and do not paraphrase”</span>. The remaining instructions are kept identical to ensure the model strictly avoids generating extraneous conversational content.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Experimental Setup</h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We utilize Whisper-Large-v3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite> as the base ASR model, Voxtral-Mini-3B-2507 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>]</cite> as the Audio LLM corrector, and DeBERTa-v3-Base <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite> for model-based filtering. To ensure parameter efficiency, we employ Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite> with rank <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>16</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">16</annotation></semantics></math>, scaling <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>32</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">32</annotation></semantics></math>, and dropout <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.05" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.05</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.05</annotation></semantics></math>. Both ASR and LLM backbones utilize 4-bit quantization (QLoRA) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite> with adapters applied to the ASR decoder and LLM language model, while the filter uses standard LoRA on its encoder. Training runs for <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5</annotation></semantics></math> epochs with a global batch size of <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="128" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>128</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">128</annotation></semantics></math> and a cosine scheduler (<math id="S4.SS4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10\%</annotation></semantics></math> warmup), using peak learning rates of <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5\times 10^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5\times 10^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math> for ASR, <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math> for the LLM, and <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10^{-3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^{-3}</annotation></semantics></math> for the model filter. During inference, we employ greedy decoding for ASR and beam search (width <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5</annotation></semantics></math>) for the LLM. For rule-based filtering, we discard corrections if the character error rate (CER) exceeds <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.15" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.15</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.15</annotation></semantics></math>, the length ratio falls outside <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0.95,1.15]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0.95</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1.15</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0.95,1.15]</annotation></semantics></math>, the unique token ratio is below <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.40" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.40</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.40</annotation></semantics></math>, or if digit mismatches exceed <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math>. We evaluate ReHear against iterative supervised learning (ISL) and two variants of iterative pseudo-labeling (IPL) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>, <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite>: a standard naive IPL utilizing raw ASR hypotheses, and a robust rule-filtered IPL. For the latter, we apply strict criteria to retain only high-quality pseudo-labels: confidence at least <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.95" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.95</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.95</annotation></semantics></math>, speaking rate within <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[2.0,5.0]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>2.0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5.0</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[2.0,5.0]</annotation></semantics></math> words/sec, and compression ratio at least <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.5</annotation></semantics></math>. For each configuration, we conduct <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5</annotation></semantics></math> independent runs with <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3</annotation></semantics></math> iterations, selecting the checkpoint with the lowest validation WER. All reported WER metrics are computed after standard text normalization, which includes lowercasing, removing punctuation, and stripping common filler words. We implement our framework using PyTorch <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>, <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite> and the Hugging Face ecosystem <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>, <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>, <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>, <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>, <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>, <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>]</cite>, alongside tools for audio processing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>, <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>, <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>]</cite> and evaluation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>, <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>]</cite>. All experiments were conducted on <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>8</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8</annotation></semantics></math> NVIDIA A100 GPUs.</p>
</div>
</section>

</table>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As presented in Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.5 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ReHear: Iterative Pseudo-Label Refinement for Semi-SupervisedSpeech Recognition via Audio Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, traditional iterative pseudo-labeling (IPL) often struggles to improve upon the supervised baseline (ISL), particularly on challenging datasets like Earnings and AMI where confirmation bias leads to performance degradation. Even when incorporating strict rule-based filtering (IPL + Rule) to reject confident errors, the method fails to consistently outperform the supervised baseline. In contrast, ReHear successfully mitigates this issue, consistently outperforming both ISL and IPL baselines across all benchmarks by leveraging audio-aware LLM corrections to generate high-fidelity targets. This capability effectively unlocks the potential of abundant unlabeled data, providing a cost-efficient solution for domains where manual annotation is expensive. Detailed analysis reveals that the proposed framework is particularly effective in complex acoustic environments, such as the spontaneous financial narratives in Earnings-21/22 and the multi-speaker meeting scenarios in AMI, achieving substantial WER reductions on both labeled and unlabeled sets. Even on SPGISpeech, where the baseline is already accurate, our method yields further gains. Regarding filtering strategies, rule-based constraints (ReHear + Rule) yield the highest stability, while the learned model filter (ReHear + Model) also delivers competitive results, albeit slightly constrained by overfitting on limited labeled data. Notably, standard ReHear without additional filtering remains highly robust and frequently surpasses filtered IPL, demonstrating that the audio-aware corrector significantly reduces the dependency on complex post-hoc filtering mechanisms.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.6 </span>Ablation Studies</h3>

<div id="S4.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To investigate the contribution of specific design choices, we conduct ablation studies on the Earnings-21 dataset, reporting all results using the standard ReHear framework without additional filtering mechanisms.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS6.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.6.1 </span>Modality and Position</h4>

<div id="S4.SS6.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS6.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We analyze the contribution of acoustic features and their positional encoding within the input sequence. As presented in Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.6.1 Modality and Position ‣ 4.6 Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ReHear: Iterative Pseudo-Label Refinement for Semi-SupervisedSpeech Recognition via Audio Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, relying solely on the textual hypothesis (text-only) results in substantially higher error rates, indicating that without acoustic grounding, the LLM acts merely as a grammatical editor unable to rectify phonetic errors. In contrast, incorporating audio leads to substantial gains across both settings. Notably, prefixing the hypothesis with audio embeddings (audio + text) achieves the best performance on both sets. This suggests that conditioning the model on the source speech before presenting the potentially erroneous text facilitates more effective error detection and correction.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 3: </span>Ablation study on input modality and positioning using Earnings-21. <section id="S4.SS6.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.6.2 </span>Decoding Strategies</h4>

<div id="S4.SS6.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS6.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate the impact of different decoding strategies on the quality of Audio LLM-generated corrections. As shown in Table <a href="#S4.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 4.6.2 Decoding Strategies ‣ 4.6 Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ReHear: Iterative Pseudo-Label Refinement for Semi-SupervisedSpeech Recognition via Audio Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, deterministic beam search consistently yields significantly lower error rates compared to greedy decoding and stochastic temperature sampling (<math id="S4.SS6.SSS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=0.7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.7</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=0.7</annotation></semantics></math>). The inferior performance of sampling suggests that introducing randomness is detrimental to the error correction task, where fidelity to the source audio is paramount over generation diversity. In contrast, beam search facilitates a more effective exploration of the hypothesis space. While a beam width of <math id="S4.SS6.SSS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=3</annotation></semantics></math> achieves the lowest WER on the labeled test set, increasing the width to <math id="S4.SS6.SSS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=5</annotation></semantics></math> results in the best performance on the unlabeled set. Consequently, we employ beam search to ensure the generation of robust and acoustically grounded pseudo-labels.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T4" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 4: </span>Ablation study on LLM decoding strategies using Earnings-21. <section id="S4.SS6.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.6.3 </span>Iterative Dynamics</h4>

<div id="S4.SS6.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS6.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We investigate the impact of the self-training loop depth on performance using the Earnings-21 dataset. To mitigate potential overfitting and noise accumulation during iterative updates, we introduce a decay strategy where the learning rate is halved and the number of training epochs is decremented by one at each subsequent iteration. As shown in Table <a href="#S4.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 4.6.3 Iterative Dynamics ‣ 4.6 Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ ReHear: Iterative Pseudo-Label Refinement for Semi-SupervisedSpeech Recognition via Audio Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, pseudo-labeling gains are realized rapidly. While the standard ReHear approach begins to degrade after the second iteration, the decay mechanism effectively stabilizes training, maintaining robust performance over prolonged iterations. Notably, the WER reduction saturates around the second iteration. Consequently, extending the loop beyond this point yields diminishing returns, justifying our choice of setting the limit to <math id="S4.SS6.SSS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3</annotation></semantics></math> iterations for the main experiments to balance computational efficiency and performance stability.</p>
</div>

<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we introduced a semi-supervised framework that employs instruction-tuned audio-aware large language models for speech recognition correction and iterative pseudo-labeling. By grounding the correction process directly in acoustic features, our method generates high-quality supervision signals that surpass those derived from filtered pseudo-labels and text-only correction. Empirical evaluations across multiple datasets confirm that this framework consistently outperforms both supervised benchmarks and traditional pseudo-labeling techniques. Our analysis further demonstrates that incorporating audio context is the decisive factor in reducing recognition errors, offering a data-efficient pathway for enhancing system performance using unlabeled speech.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>

    <p><strong>Tip:</strong> You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.</p>
    <p>Our team has already identified <a class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/arXiv/html_feedback/issues"
        target="_blank">the following issues</a>. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we
      may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability
      should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
      all.</p>
